claim: The Cricket Paralysis Virus employs an Internal Ribosomal Entry Site (CrPV-IRES) to express its structural genes in the late stage of infection.
source: The Cricket Paralysis Virus employs an Internal Ribosomal Entry Site (CrPV-IRES) to express its structural genes in the late stage of infection.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of CrPV-IRES that draws from established knowledge about viral translation mechanisms.

claim: Ribosome hijacking by CrPV-IRES is achieved by molecular mimicry to tRNA and mRNA.
source: Ribosome hijacking is achieved by a sophisticated use of molecular mimicry to tRNA and mRNA, employed to manipulate intrinsically dynamic components of the ribosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript showing tRNA mimicry.

claim: Binding and translocation through the ribosome is required for CrPV-IRES to initiate translation.
source: Binding and translocation through the ribosome is required for this IRES to initiate translation.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two structures of a double translocated CrPV-IRES with aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site were solved by single particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryoEM).
source: We report two structures, solved by single particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryoEM), of a double translocated CrPV-IRES with aminoacyl-tRNA in the peptidyl site (P site) of the ribosome.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental work performed, supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CrPV-IRES adopts a previously unseen conformation, mimicking the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA.
source: CrPV-IRES adopts a previously unseen conformation, mimicking the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript showing the novel conformation.

claim: The structures suggest a mechanism for the positioning of the first aminoacyl-tRNA shared with the distantly related Hepatitis C Virus IRES.
source: The structures suggest a mechanism for the positioning of the first aminoacyl-tRNA shared with the distantly related Hepatitis C Virus IRES.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the structural data with known HCV-IRES structures.

claim: Translation initiation is the most complex and highly regulated step of protein synthesis.
source: Translation initiation is the most complex and highly regulated step of protein synthesis (Schmeing and Ramakrishnan, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Canonical initiation results in the formation of an elongation-competent ribosome with an aminoacyl-tRNA base paired with mRNA at the P site.
source: Canonical initiation results in the formation of an elongation-competent ribosome with an aminoacyl-tRNA base paired with messenger RNA (mRNA)at the peptidyl site (P site) of the ribosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about canonical translation initiation.

claim: Most eukaryotic mRNAs contain a unique nucleotide structure at their 5' end, known as the cap structure.
source: Most eukaryotic mRNAs contain a unique nucleotide structure at their 5' end, known as the cap structure.
evidence: This is established knowledge about eukaryotic mRNA structure.

claim: The multi-subunit initiation factor eIF4F binds the cap structure and recruits the 43S complex.
source: The multi-subunit initiation factor eIF4F binds the cap structure and recruits the 43S complex consisting of the small ribosomal subunit (40S), eIF2/GTP/Met-tRNAMet ternary complex, eIF3, eIF1, eIF1A, and eIF5 (Jackson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The 43S complex scans the 5'-untranslated region of the mRNA downstream to the initiation codon.
source: The attached 43S complex scans the 5'-untranslated region of the mRNA downstream to the initiation codon, where it forms the 48S initiation complex with the established codon-anticodon base-pairing in the ribosomal P site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the scanning mechanism in eukaryotic translation initiation.

claim: eIF5B promotes the recruitment of the large ribosomal subunit (60S) and the formation of the elongation-competent 80S ribosome.
source: Finally, eIF5B, the eukaryotic ortholog of the bacterial initiation factor 2 (IF2), promotes the recruitment of the large ribosomal subunit (60S) and the formation of the elongation-competent 80S ribosome (Fernández et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Eukaryotic viruses have evolved refined molecular strategies to interfere with canonical initiation factors, leading to the hijacking of host ribosomes.
source: Eukaryotic viruses have evolved refined molecular strategies to interfere with canonical initiation factors, leading to the hijacking of host ribosomes to produce viral proteins (Jackson et al., 2010; Hertz and Thompson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: A common strategy used by different types of viruses relies on structured RNA sequences at the ends of their mRNAs called Internal Ribosomal Entry Sites (IRES).
source: A common strategy used by different types of viruses relies on structured RNA sequences at the ends of their mRNAs (Filbin and Kieft, 2009).These sequences are called Internal Ribosomal Entry Sites (IRES) and form specific three-dimensional structures able to manipulate and co-opt the host translational machinery (Yamamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: IRES sequences are classified according to the subset of factors they require for initiation.
source: IRES sequences are classified according to the subset of factors they require for initiation (Filbin and Kieft, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Type IV IRES sequences, including the Cricket Paralysis Virus IRES (CrPV-IRES) and the Taura Syndrome Virus IRES (TSV-IRES) do not require initiation factors.
source: Type IV IRES sequences, including the Cricket Paralysis Virus IRES (CrPV-IRES) and the Taura Syndrome Virus IRES (TSV-IRES) do not require initiation factors and are the best studied IRESs.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited literature.

claim: Type IV IRESs are approximately 200-nucleotide-long sequences.
source: Biochemical and structural studies have provided a detailed view on how these approximately 200-nucleotide-long sequences interact with and manipulate the ribosome (Wilson et al., 2000; Spahn et al., 2004; Petrov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature describing these IRESs.

claim: A modular architecture of three pseudoknots (PKI, PKII and PKIII) is crucial for type IV IRESs to establish a balance between structural flexibility and rigidity.
source: A modular architecture of three pseudoknots (PKI, PKII and PKIII, Figure 1A) is crucial for these IRESs to establish a balance between structural flexibility and rigidity, essential for interaction with the ribosome and with two elongation factors (eEF2 and eEF1A) required for IRES translocation through the ribosome (Jan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1A showing the structure.

claim: PKI mimics an anti-codon stem loop (ASL) of a tRNA interacting with its cognate mRNA codon.
source: PKI mimics an anti-codon stem loop (ASL) of a tRNA interacting with its cognate mRNA codon, and plays an essential role in setting up the correct reading frame in the aminoacyl site (A site) of the ribosome (Costantino et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: A ribosome primed with a type IV IRES alternates between rotated and non-rotated configurations of the small ribosomal subunit.
source: A ribosome primed with a type IV IRES alternates between rotated and non-rotated configurations of the small ribosomal subunit (Fernández et al., 2014; Koh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: After peptidyl-transfer in canonical translocation, the ribosome alternates between rotated and non-rotated configurations of the small ribosomal subunit with respect to the large ribosomal subunit.
source: Similarly, after peptidyl-transfer in canonical translocation, the ribosome alternates between rotated and non-rotated configurations of the small ribosomal subunit with respect to the large ribosomal subunit (Voorhees and Ramakrishnan, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: The pre-translocation stage of the ribosome is recognized by a protein translocation factor (EF-G in Bacteria, eEF2 in Eukarya).
source: This pre-translocation stage of the ribosome is recognized by a protein translocation factor (EF-G in Bacteria, eEF2 in Eukarya), which in GTP-bound form induces an additional rotation of the small subunit and blocks the A site of the ribosome (Tourigny et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Translocation proceeds forward by a back rotation of the small subunit to recover a canonical configuration of the ribosome.
source: Translocation proceeds forward by a back rotation of the small subunit to recover a canonical configuration of the ribosome. This is accomplished by a swiveling movement of the head of the small subunit in an orthogonal direction respect to that of the rotation of the small subunit (Ratje et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: The back-rotation of the small subunit accompanied by the swiveling of the head is performed while EF-G/eEF2 are still bound.
source: The back-rotation of the small subunit accompanied by the swiveling of the head is performed while EF-G/eEF2 are still bound (Ramrath et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: Once the translocation factor EF-G/eEF2 leaves the ribosome, the head of the small subunit returns to its non-swiveled configuration.
source: Once the translocation factor EF-G/eEF2 leaves the ribosome, the head of the small subunit returns to its non-swiveled configuration, rendering a ribosome primed with a peptidyl-tRNA in the P site, a deacylated tRNA in the E site and a vacant A site ready to accept the next aminoacyl-tRNA (Noller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: The L1 stalk contributes to the vectorial movement of tRNAs, offering additional anchoring points to the leaving deacylated-tRNA in the E site.
source: The L1 stalk, a component of the large ribosomal subunit, also contribute to the vectorial movement of tRNAs, offering additional anchoring points to the leaving deacylated-tRNA in the E site (Fei et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claim: The movements of the L1 stalk are coordinated with those of the small subunit.
source: The movements of the L1 stalk are coordinated with those of the small subunit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome dynamics.

claim: Type IV IRESs require two translocation events to place the first aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site.
source: Type IV IRESs require two translocation events to place the first aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site making use of the intrinsic dynamic elements of the ribosome involved in canonical translocation (Murray et al., 2016; Abeyrathne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: Less is known about the second translocation event required for the first aminoacyl-tRNA to enter the P site.
source: However, less is known about the second translocation event, required for the first aminoacyl-tRNA to enter the P site, ending the unusual initiation pathway followed by this type of IRESs.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, providing context for the current study.

claim: Two related states of the mammalian ribosome with a double translocated CrPV-IRES and P site aminoacyl-tRNA were visualized at 3.2 and 4.75 Ångstroms resolution.
source: We report the visualization by means of single-particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryoEM) of two related states of the mammalian ribosome with a double translocated CrPV-IRES and P site aminoacyl-tRNA at 3.2 and 4.75 Ångstroms resolution.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The head swiveling of the small ribosomal subunit plays a fundamental role in the late step of the second translocation event.
source: The head swiveling of the small ribosomal subunit plays a fundamental role in the late step of this translocation event, inducing a remarkable conformational change on the PKI of the CrPV-IRES, which becomes disassembled, to mimic the acceptor stem of a E site tRNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data presented.

claim: A pre-translocation complex assembled by mixing of CrPV-IRES with 40S and 60S subunits results in a +14–15 nt toe-print signal from the CCU.
source: A pre-translocation complex, assembled by mixing of CrPV-IRES with 40S and 60S subunits, results in a +14–15 nt toe-print signal from the CCU (sequence belonging to the PKI) and thus indicate the presence of PKI in the ribosomal A site (Figure 1C, lane 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The addition of elongation factors leads to a 5–6 nucleotides toe-print shift showing the double translocation event.
source: The addition of elongation factors leads to a 5–6 nucleotides toe-print shift showing the double translocation event (Figure 1C, lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mutation of the first sense codon to a stop codon and the addition of the release factor 1 (eRF1) were applied to prevent spontaneous back-translocation of the IRES.
source: In this report, the mutation of the first sense codon to a stop codon and the addition of the release factor 1 (eRF1) were applied to prevent spontaneous back-translocation of the IRES.
evidence: This describes the experimental strategy used in the study, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The supplementation of the reaction with a mutated and catalytically inactive version of the release factor 1 (eRF1*, AGQ mutation) causes a +20 nt toe-print signal from the first sense codon (leucine CUU codon) in the P site.
source: The supplementation of the reaction with a mutated and catalytically inactive version of the release factor 1 (eRF1*, AGQ mutation) causes a +20 nt toe-print signal from the first sense codon (leucine CUU codon) in the P site, which is in a good agreement with previous report (Muhs et al., 2015), indicating proper binding of eRF1* (Figure 1C, lane 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to previous work.

claim: Maximum likelihood particle sorting methods implemented in RELION were applied to a large cryoEM dataset at two different stages.
source: Maximum likelihood particle sorting methods implemented in RELION (Scheres, 2012) were applied to a large cryoEM dataset at two different stages (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the computational methods used, supported by citation and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: An initial classification in two dimensions allowed for the separation of full ribosome (80S) from small subunit (40S) particles.
source: An initial classification in two dimensions allowed for the separation of full ribosome (80S) from small subunit (40S) particles.
evidence: This describes the data processing workflow.

claim: A binary 80S/CrPV-IRES complex in a pre-translocation conformation could be identified as well as two sub-populations with CrPV-IRES in a double translocated state.
source: A binary 80S/CrPV-IRES complex in a pre-translocation conformation could be identified as well as two sub-populations with CrPV-IRES in a double translocated state.
evidence: This describes the results of the classification analysis.

claim: In the double translocated reconstructions, the ribosome adopts a non-rotated configuration of the small subunit, with clear density for aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site and either eEF2 or eRF1* in the A site.
source: In the double translocated reconstructions, the ribosome adopts a non-rotated configuration of the small subunit, with clear density for aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site and a either eEF2 or eRF1* in the A site (Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figures and table.

claim: Recent studies by single-molecule FRET (smFRET) have characterized the kinetics of the translocation events required for the CrPV-IRES to deliver an aminoacyl-tRNA to the P site of the ribosome.
source: Recent studies by single-molecule FRET (smFRET) have characterized the kinetics of the translocation events required for the CrPV-IRES to deliver an aminoacyl-tRNA to the P site of the ribosome (Petrov et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature.

claim: Slow movements of the CrPV-IRES compared with canonical translocation of tRNAs are evident from smFRET data.
source: Slow movements of the CrPV-IRES compared with canonical translocation of tRNAs are evident from this data and explain the capturing of a late-stage intermediate of translocation with eEF2 in our dataset (Figure 2A-C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited smFRET data and the current structural data.

claim: The conformation of the IRES in the intermediate state with eEF2 is similar to the conformation reported for the single translocated state.
source: Our cryoEM reconstruction reveals that the conformation of the IRES in this intermediate state is similar to the conformation reported for the single translocated state (Muhs et al., 2015), with the SL-IV and SL-V detached from the 40S and exposed to the solvent.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previously published structures.

claim: PKI is in an intermediate position between the P and E sites of the small subunit in the eEF2-bound complex.
source: PKI is in an intermediate position between the P and E sites of the small subunit as well as the aminoacyl-tRNA is in an intermediate position between the A and P site of the 40S (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Domain IV of eEF2 occupies the A site of the small ribosomal subunit.
source: Domain IV of eEF2 occupies the A site of the small ribosomal subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented.

claim: The configuration with eEF2 is maintained by a distinctive swiveled configuration of the 40S head.
source: This configuration is maintained by a distinctive swiveled configuration of the 40S head, resembling one of the late stages recently reported for the first translocation event (Figure 2C)(Abeyrathne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and comparison with previously published structures.

claim: The most populated class of particles represent a double translocated CrPV-IRES with aminoacyl-tRNA in a canonical configuration in the P site and eRF1* in the A site.
source: The most populated class of particles represent a double translocated CrPV-IRES with aminoacyl-tRNA in a canonical configuration in the P site and eRF1* in the A site (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the results of the particle classification analysis.

claim: Both aminoacyl-tRNA and eRF1* populate conformations recently described, with the characteristic bent of the mRNA at the stop codon.
source: Both aminoacyl-tRNA and eRF1* populate conformations recently described, with the characteristic bent of the mRNA at the stop codon (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D; Brown et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and comparison with previously published structures.

claim: The small subunit in the eRF1*-containing reconstruction is in a non-rotated configuration and the 40S head is not tilted or swiveled.
source: The small subunit in this reconstruction is in a non-rotated configuration and the 40S head is not tilted or swiveled (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CrPV-IRES has undergone a conformational change that mainly affects PKI, but also the relative orientation of PKII and PKIII.
source: CrPV-IRES has undergone a conformational change that mainly affects PKI, but also the relative orientation of PKII and PKIII.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented.

claim: In the pre-translocated and single translocated conformation of the IRES, PKII and PKIII interact by a network of non-covalent interactions involving sugar–sugar stacking interactions as well as A-minor interactions.
source: In the pre-translocated as well as in the single translocated conformation of the IRES, PKII and PKIII interact by a network of non-covalent interactions involving sugar–sugar stacking interactions as well as A-minor interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, (Murray et al., 2016; Pfingsten et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and citations to previous work.

claim: The compact configuration adopted due to the physical proximity of PKII and PKIII seems to be a requirement for the initial binding to the ribosome as well as for the first translocation event.
source: This compact configuration adopted due to the physical proximity of PKII and PKIII seems to be a requirement for the initial binding to the ribosome as well as for the first translocation event (Murray et al., 2016; Muhs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In the double translocated state, the interactions between PKII and PKIII are no longer established and a pronounced gap could be observed between both pseudoknots.
source: In the state described here, these interactions are no longer established and a pronounced gap could be observed between both pseudoknots (Figure 4B, bottom right and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Upon back-swiveling of the 40S following eEF2 departure, the aminoacyl-tRNA is placed in its final canonical position in the P site.
source: Upon back-swiveling of the 40S following eEF2 departure, the aminoacyl-tRNA is placed in its final canonical position in the P site (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data.

claim: Back-swiveling of the 40S triggers the disassembly of the CrPV-IRES PKI.
source: This event triggers the disassembly of the CrPV-IRES PKI.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data.

claim: The mRNA-like part of PKI remains placed in the E site of the 40S after disassembly.
source: Although the mRNA-like part remains placed in the E site of the 40S, the ASL-like segment experiences a pronounced displacement to occupy the E site of the 60S, now mimicking the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA (Figure 3B C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ASL-like segment of PKI experiences a pronounced displacement to occupy the E site of the 60S, mimicking the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA.
source: Although the mRNA-like part remains placed in the E site of the 40S, the ASL-like segment experiences a pronounced displacement to occupy the E site of the 60S, now mimicking the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA (Figure 3B C).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The L1.1 part of CrPV-IRES remains attached to the L1 stalk along the translocation process.
source: The L1.1 part of CrPV-IRES remains attached to the L1 stalk along this process whose position relative to the 60S is similar to the one described in the complex with eEF2 and a non-hydrolyzable GTP analog or after the first translocation (Figure 4A)(Murray et al., 2016; Muhs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and comparison with previously published structures.

claim: In the swiveled configuration, SL-IV and SL-V are exposed to the solvent, in a similar position described for the single translocated CrPV-IRES.
source: The swiveled configuration (Figure 4B, left), SL-IV and SL-V, components of PKII, are exposed to the solvent, in a similar position described for the single translocated CrPV-IRES (Muhs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and comparison with previously published structures.

claim: The eukaryotic specific protein eS25 is a key element of the small subunit involved in early recruitment of the CrPV-IRES as well as in the positioning of the IRES in the pre-translocation stage.
source: The eukaryotic specific protein eS25, a key element of the small subunit involved in early recruitment of the CrPV-IRES as well as in the positioning of the IRES in the pre-translocation stage (Schüler et al., 2006), is not interacting with the IRES (Figure 4B, left arrow).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the swiveled configuration, eS25 is not interacting with the IRES.
source: The eukaryotic specific protein eS25, a key element of the small subunit involved in early recruitment of the CrPV-IRES as well as in the positioning of the IRES in the pre-translocation stage (Schüler et al., 2006), is not interacting with the IRES (Figure 4B, left arrow).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Upon back swiveling of the 40S head, a new interaction is established between the CrPV-IRES and eS25.
source: Upon back swiveling of the 40S head, a new interaction is established between the CrPV-IRES and eS25 (Figure 4B right,arrow and (C) not involving SL-V like in the pre-translocated complex.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The α-helix of eS25 comprising residues 52 to 65 could be observed in interacting distance with a helical segment of the CrPV-IRES formed by residues 6123–6127 and 6159–6164.
source: The α-helix of eS25 comprising residues 52 to 65 could be observed in interacting distance with a helical segment of the CrPV-IRES formed by residues 6123–6127 and 6159–6164 (Figure 4C, top right).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The new interaction with eS25 stabilizes the CrPV-IRES in a distinctive conformation, with PKII and PKIII assembled but with a wider relative orientation.
source: This new interaction stabilizes the CrPV-IRES in a distinctive conformation, with PKII and PKIII assembled but with a wider relative orientation (Figure 4C) and the PKI disassembled with residues 6175 to 6200 (Figure 3C)corresponding to the ASL mimicking part of PKI, populating a space corresponding to the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA (Figure 4C, bottom right and Video 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: CrPV-IRES initially assembles a binary 80S/CrPV-IRES complex by either directly recruiting empty 80S or by a step-wise pathway in which CrPV-IRES first recruits the 40S subunit and then the 60S subunit.
source: As suggested by classic cross-linking experiments (Pestova et al., 2004), smFRET data ( Petrov et al., 2016) and cryoEM reconstructions (Spahn et al., 2004; Murray et al., 2016), CrPV-IRES initially assembles a binary 80S/CrPV-IRES complex by either directly recruiting empty 80S or by a step-wise pathway in which CrPV-IRES first recruits the 40S subunit and then the 60S subunit (Figure 5, bottom left).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Once the binary 80S/CrPV-IRES is assembled, the 40S oscillates between rotated and non-rotated states, with PKI inserted in the A site and minimum changes in the overall conformation of the IRES.
source: Once the binary 80S/CrPV-IRES is assembled, the 40S oscillates between rotated and non-rotated states, with PKI inserted in the A site and minimum changes in the overall conformation of the IRES (Fernández et al., 2014; Koh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: These movements are coupled to oscillations of the L1 stalk.
source: These movements are coupled to oscillations of the L1 stalk.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosome dynamics.

claim: The rotated state is the substrate of eEF2, which, in its GTP-bound form, induces an additional rotation of the small subunit and additional displacement of the L1 stalk.
source: The rotated state is the substrate of eEF2, which, in its GTP-bound form, induces an additional rotation of the small subunit and additional displacement of the L1 stalk, to facilitate the translocation of the PKI from the A to the P site (Figure 5A, top left).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data and established knowledge.

claim: Back rotation and back swiveling of the 40S, combined with ribosome-induced GTP hydrolysis by eEF2 results in the first translocation event of the CrPV-IRES.
source: Back rotation and back swiveling of the 40S, combined with ribosome-induced GTP hydrolysis by eEF2 results in the first translocation event of the CrPV-IRES, positioning PKI in the P site, mimicking a translocated, canonical aminoacyl-tRNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data and established knowledge about translocation.

claim: The single translocated intermediate is unstable and prone to back-translocation unless a cognate aminoacyl-tRNA captures the frame in the A site of the ribosome.
source: This intermediate is unstable and prone to back-translocation (Muhs et al., 2015), unless a cognate aminoacyl-tRNA, delivered to the ribosome in complex with eEF1A and GTP, captures the frame in the A site of the ribosome (Petrov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Formation of the complex with aminoacyl-tRNA in the A site is a rate-limiting step in this kinetically driven process.
source: Formation of this complex is a rate-limiting step in this kinetically driven process (Petrov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the single translocated IRES state, SL-IV and SL-V are solvent exposed, the PKI occupy the P site of the 40S and an aminoacyl-tRNA occupies the A site.
source: In the single translocated IRES state, SL-IV and SL-V, which are initially attached to the ribosome, are solvent exposed, the PKI occupy the P site of the 40S and an aminoacyl-tRNA occupies the A site.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data and previous work.

claim: The single translocated state will oscillate between rotated and non-rotated configurations of the small subunit as a canonical pre-translocation complex with tRNAs.
source: It is reasonable to assume this state will oscillate between rotated and non-rotated configurations of the small subunit as a canonical pre-translocation complex with tRNAs (Budkevich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy with canonical translation and supported by citation.

claim: The second translocation step is required to place the first aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site and thus finish the initiation phase of translation.
source: The second translocation step is required to place the first aminoacyl-tRNA in the P site and thus finish the initiation phase of translation (Figure 5A, bottom right).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CrPV-IRES mechanism.

claim: CrPV-IRES translocation should be coupled with the movement of the aminoacyl-tRNA occupying the A site during the second translocation.
source: At this stage, CrPV-IRES translocation should be coupled with the movement of the aminoacyl-tRNA occupying the A site, and this seems to happen with a conformation of the IRES similar to the one reported for the first translocation (Muhs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data and comparison with previous work.

claim: The IRES conformation is maintained until the very last moment as the intermediate captured with eEF2 presents a back-rotated configuration of the 40S.
source: This conformation is maintained until the very last moment as the intermediate captured here with eEF2 presents a back-rotated configuration of the 40S (Abeyrathne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data and comparison with previous work.

claim: A pronounced swiveling of the 40S head is in place in the eEF2-bound intermediate, probably induced by the presence of eEF2.
source: However, a pronounced swiveling of the 40S head is in place, probably induced by the presence of eEF2 (Abeyrathne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural data and comparison with previous work.

claim: Once eEF2 leaves, the back-swiveling movement of the 40S head triggers a dramatic conformational change in the CrPV-IRES with PKI disassembling.
source: Once eEF2 leaves, the back-swiveling movement of the 40S head triggers a dramatic conformational change in the CrPV-IRES: PKI is disassembled resulting in the ASL-like segment relocating to mimic the acceptor stem of a canonical E site tRNA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the two structural states.

claim: The conformational changes in the PKI upon back swiveling are combined with a reconfiguration of the relative positioning of PKII and PKIII.
source: These conformational changes in the PKI of the CrPV-IRES upon back swiveling are combined with a reconfiguration of the relative positioning of PKII and PKIII.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data.

claim: The new conformation is stabilized by a newly reported IRES/40S interaction with the ribosomal protein eS25.
source: This new conformation is stabilized by a newly reported IRES/40S interaction with the ribosomal protein eS25, which is also involved in the early recruitment of the IRES to the 40S (Murray et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and citation to previous work.
